There are several ways to use docker.
- Distributed image: yes, you need to copy the files.  Building the image would then be part of the github actions put in place for the project and may use a specific Dockerfile.
  The intent would then be to not fetch the github repository at all.
- Local git clone (for debug/other adjustments),
  - Build the image locally using a Docker file;
  - Run the prebuilt image, but override some contents using a "-volume .:/app" option for instance.
  - These methods could be managed together with a "docker-compose.yaml" file which IMHO avoids OS dependent scripts.
  - Build the image locally - this seemed to be the purpose of the Dockerfile that I was using as it was called "measure_local".

This Dockerfile is already using an image "python:3.8-slim-buster" so the local build is quite limited.  
The intent of the 'runDocker' script is clearly to run it locally.  
In order for the 'runDocker' script to work, the repository has to be locally extracted.

Therefore, the argument that the COPY not needed to build the image as the goal is to run things locally.

Mounting the local directory in the container is proposed in the Docker-compose Getting Started guide: https://docs.docker.com/compose/gettingstarted/#step-5-edit-the-compose-file-to-add-a-bind-mount .

That still allows to use a prebuilt image because even if there is already contents for the '/app' directory,  a mount '.:/app' will override the contents with the local contents.

It's considered bad practice to repeat the same string twice and check for string values in if statements.
These should be constants or enums.
Enums are relatively new in Python but exists in many other languages. 
The idea is to create an enumaration (list) of possible values.

You can create an enum by subclassing `StrEnum`. See [here](https://github.com/bramstroker/homeassistant-powercalc/blob/master/custom_components/powercalc/const.py#L157) for some examples where I use it as well.
So you can add an `DeviceType` enum.
Also you can include all enum values automatically in the inquirer list `[cls.value for cls in DeviceType]`

So that means when a device type is added we only have to add a new value to the enum.

In the if statements you can check `device == DeviceType.LIGHT` for example. When an invalid enum value is passed an error will be raise. Also your IDE (pycharm, visual studio) will do autocompletion.

So you see a lot of advantages for clear and consise code.

As explained (maybe a bit convoluted) [here](https://github.com/bramstroker/homeassistant-powercalc/issues/2663).

So in short:

Z2M does matching based on ZigBee manufacturer and ZigBee device type, and replaces both with something like “Lidl” and “HG08131B”.

But as soon as the second device is added by a manufacturer, the device type is changed to a list, to something like "[HG07834A/HG09155A](https://www.zigbee2mqtt.io/devices/HG07834A_HG09155A.html#lidl-hg07834a%252Fhg09155a)" and simple matching of the name does not work anymore.

So users are never informed, that there's a matching profile for their device.

The best solution would be, IMHO to show "hey there's maybe a profile available for your device" and then show a list of the 2-3 devices which match the identifier.

The solutions to achieve this are:

- Recommending users to set "Include device information" under MQTT in z2m, so Zigbee info is passed through as additional fields. Those are stable and could be matched.
- Separate the string list send by z2m (and ZHA) and match each of those, to search for the devices powercalc has in it's library. And if there's any match, show this to the user as option.
- Add aliases each time z2m/zha changes the string lists for the device (probably the worst one, as we need to keep updating the strings all the time).

I recommend a dual approach: Add ZigBee device type and manufacturer to the device profiles and if they are present in the device, search for them. This allows the best matching, as those are stable.

If that's not available, match the manufacturer and then separate the string lists and match each of those.

```python
def take_average_measurement(self, duration: int, measure_resistance: bool = False) -> float:
    """Measures average power or resistance over a specified duration."""
    _LOGGER.info(
        "Measuring average %s over %s seconds",
        "resistance" if measure_resistance else "power",
        duration,
    )
    start_time = time.time()
    readings: list[float] = []

    while (time.time() - start_time) < duration:
        if not self._can_continue_measurement(start_time, duration):
            break

        time.sleep(self.config.sleep_time)
        measurement = self._perform_measurement(measure_resistance)
        
        if measurement is not None:
            readings.append(measurement)

    if not readings:
        _LOGGER.error("No valid readings were recorded.")
        exit(1)

    average = round(mean(readings), 2)
    unit = "Ω" if measure_resistance else "W"
    _LOGGER.info("Average of %d measurements: %.2f %s", len(readings), average, unit)
    return average

def _can_continue_measurement(self, start_time: float, duration: int) -> bool:
    """Checks if the measurement can continue based on elapsed time."""
    return (time.time() - start_time + self.config.sleep_time) < duration

def _perform_measurement(self, measure_resistance: bool) -> float | None:
    """Performs a single measurement and returns the result."""
    if measure_resistance:
        return self._measure_resistance()

    if self.dummy_load_value:
        return self._measure_power_with_dummy_load()

    return self._measure_power_without_dummy_load()

def _measure_resistance(self) -> float | None:
    """Measures resistance based on voltage and power."""
    result = self.power_meter.get_power(include_voltage=True)
    power, voltage = result.power, result.voltage

    if voltage < 1:
        _LOGGER.error("Error: Voltage measurement returned zero. Aborting measurement.")
        exit(1)

    if round(power, 2) == 0:
        _LOGGER.warning("Invalid measurement: power: %.2f W, voltage: %.2f", power, voltage)
        return None

    resistance = round((voltage**2) / power, 4)
    _LOGGER.debug("Measured resistance: %.2f Ω; power: %.2f W, voltage: %.2f", resistance, power, voltage)
    return resistance

def _measure_power_with_dummy_load(self) -> float | None:
    """Measures power with the dummy load value accounted for."""
    self._validate_voltage_support()
    result = self.power_meter.get_power(include_voltage=True)
    power, voltage = result.power, result.voltage

    if voltage < 1:
        _LOGGER.error("Error: Voltage measurement returned zero. Aborting measurement.")
        exit(1)

    dummy_power = (voltage**2) / self.dummy_load_value
    power -= dummy_power

    if round(power, 2) <= 0:
        _LOGGER.warning(
            "Invalid measurement after subtracting dummy load consumption. Calculated consumption: %.2f W; ignoring",
            power,
        )
        return None

    _LOGGER.info("Measured power: %.2f W", power)
    return power

def _measure_power_without_dummy_load(self) -> float | None:
    """Measures power without the dummy load."""
    power = self.power_meter.get_power().power

    if round(power, 2) == 0:
        _LOGGER.warning("Invalid measurement. Consumption: %.2f W; ignoring", power)
        return None

    _LOGGER.info("Measured power: %.2f W", power)
    return power
```

**1. Fixed 60 s tick biases energy upward (suggest scheduling at sample expiry):**
An increment raises power immediately (battery state change), but the drop when it leaves the window waits for the next 60 s tick. On average, each increment is held ~30 s longer than `window` (i.e. about +30/window of charging energy: +5% at 600 s, +10% at 300 s). That's the "timer discretization" in the replay doc, but it's actually a systematic bias. Reproducing the replay's event + 60 s tick model on the bundle gives exactly its totals and adding a recalculation at each sample's expiry removes the bias:

| Window | Continuous | 60 s ticks (this PR) | + update at sample expiry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 300 s | +0.20% | +2.61% | +0.20% |
| 600 s | +0.04% | +1.42% | +0.04% |
| 1200 s | -0.31% | +0.37% | -0.31% |

Something like this, with the sensor (or the strategy via its update callback) arming `async_track_point_in_time` for that moment after each recalculation, keeping the 60 s tick as a safety net:
```python
def get_next_update_time(self) -> datetime | None:
    """When the oldest increment leaves the window and power must step down."""
    return self._samples[1].timestamp + self._window if len(self._samples) > 1 else None
```
See the `battery_rate.py` comment: arming a point-in-time update at the oldest sample’s expiry here, alongside the interval, removes the upward bias.

**2. Short invalid gaps clear the window:** Roborock entities can go unavailable briefly and each mid-charge blip discards up to one window (~3 Wh at 10 min). I'd suggest ignoring invalid readings and only clearing when the gap exceeds `window` or when the percentage drops across the gap.

**3. History from before docking:** Since samples keep populating while other branches are active, the window can start at a pre-docking (higher) percentage. For the Saros 10R it doesn't matter (<=0.1 points across all seven charges because the post-run wash/low-battery pause use up the window first), but a device that charges immediately on return would read low for up to one window after a short trip off the dock.
